# Rank-sensitive constants for a continuous cap cover

This is a continuous, single-body theorem. It applies fiber by fiber to
the grouped mixed-integer certificate, but does not allocate mass between
different fibers or prove OC.

Let K be a D-dimensional convex body of positive volume. Let H_i be a
finite collection of closed affine halfspaces covering R^D. Suppose
their nonzero normals span a subspace V of dimension r, 1<=r<=D. Put
gamma_j=(j/(j+1))^j for j>=1 and gamma_0=1. Then

    max_i |K intersect H_i| >= gamma_r |K|.                 (1)

If all the boundary hyperplanes share a flat F of codimension r and
F does not meet int K, the stronger conclusion is

    max_i |K intersect H_i| >= gamma_(r-1) |K|.             (2)

Both constants are sharp with D and r prescribed. No assertion that
the centroid of K has depth gamma_r is made: the point supplied below
is a center of the projected density, not necessarily that centroid.

## 1. The exact marginal and its convex negative power

Use an orthogonal continuous decomposition R^D=V+V^perp, and put
B=pi_V K. For r<D define

    f(v)=vol_(D-r){w in V^perp: v+w in K}, v in B,

and set f=0 outside B. For r=D take f=1_K. These choices are bounded,
compactly supported, upper semicontinuous, and positive on int B.
Upper semicontinuity follows by taking Hausdorff-convergent subsequences
of the bounded compact slices: each limit is contained in the limiting
slice, and volume is continuous on compact convex sets, including
lower-dimensional limits. Positivity on int B follows because the
orthogonal projection of int K is int B. For completeness, fix a point
v_0 projecting an interior point of K. Every v in int B lies strictly
between v_0 and another point of B, unless v=v_0; interpolation with
the interior point gives an interior point of K over v.

For r<D, Brunn--Minkowski and convexity of K give concavity of
f^(1/(D-r)) on its positive set. The map t -> t^(-(D-r)/(r+1)) is
convex and decreasing on (0,infinity). Therefore

    f^(-1/(r+1)) is convex,                               (3)

as an extended-real function, with infinity where f=0. Indeed the
concave inner-function inequality reverses under the decreasing outer
function, and its convexity supplies the second inequality. When
r=D, (3) is immediate for the indicator of a convex body. Positive
values on boundary slices, if present, are retained in this argument.

Orthogonal Fubini gives the exact identities

    integral f = |K|,
    |K intersect H_i| = integral_(pi_V H_i) f.              (4)

Each H_i is a cylinder in V^perp and projects to a genuine closed
halfspace of V. Their projections cover V. All their boundary
hyperplanes are null for f(v)dv; no boundary section mass is discarded.

## 2. Covering all of V

Section 2 of candidate f9c635ce5abe9f17
proves the following density theorem, using its fully proved radial
integral lemma and classical continuous Grunbaum: if f is bounded,
upper semicontinuous and compactly supported, is positive on the
interior of a full-dimensional convex support, and satisfies (3),
then some point c has every containing closed halfspace of f-mass at
least gamma_r integral f.

Its proof is needed in precisely dimension r here. The radial body
is formed at a deepest point of f. Balanced active normals ensure
that this point is also deepest in that convex radial body; ordinary
Grunbaum is applied at that body's actual centroid. Thus this use
does not replace a general density by a uniform body at an arbitrary
centroid, or assume the selected radial origin is the centroid.

At least one projected H_i contains c. Equation (4) proves (1).

## 3. Exterior common contacts for the same density class

We record explicitly the density extension of the external-contact
argument; it is not restricted to indicator functions. Suppose f on
R^r has the properties in Section 2, and all the halfspace boundaries
pass through c outside int B. They cover R^r. Then their maximum
f-mass is at least gamma_(r-1) integral f.

For r=1 the halfspaces are the two orientations of halflines based
at c; a whole-line cover contains both orientations, and one contains
all of B when c is outside its interior. This proves the assertion
with gamma_0=1, including either endpoint of B.

Let r>=2, and first assume c outside B. Translate c to zero. Strict
separation gives orthogonal coordinates (t,x) in R x R^(r-1) with
0<a<=t<=b on B. The exact central-projection density is

    phi(s)=integral_0^infinity t^(r-1) f(t,ts) dt.          (5)

The Jacobian of (t,s)->(t,ts) is t^(r-1), so phi preserves total
mass and each homogeneous cap's mass. It is bounded, upper
semicontinuous and compactly supported. Its support is convex: the
central projection of a convex set lying in t>0 is convex, as is
verified by combining original points with weights proportional to
the desired projected weights divided by their positive t-coordinates.
The same interpolation using an interior point shows positivity of
phi on the interior of that support.

Apply the radial-integral lemma in Section 1 of the cited note with
p=r to this translated f. Its hypothesis is exactly (3). The lemma
expressly allows the radial origin outside the support. Its convex
gauge restricted to the affine plane (1,s) says

    phi^(-1/r) is convex.                                (6)

The projected caps cover R^(r-1). If one is all that space, its mass
is the total mass. Otherwise remove the empty restrictions and apply
the already proved density centerpoint theorem in dimension r-1 to
phi. A cap containing the resulting point has mass at least
gamma_(r-1) integral phi. Formula (5) transfers the assertion back.

If c is on boundary B, choose a supporting normal e pointing into B
and translate all the common-contact halfspaces to c-epsilon e.
They still cover R^r, and the contact is strictly exterior. Along a
sequence epsilon decreasing to zero, one fixed cap attains the bound
infinitely often. Its indicators converge f-almost everywhere because
its limiting hyperplane is Lebesgue-null and f is bounded. Dominated
convergence proves the original closed-cap assertion.

For the body K and normal span V, the common flat is c+V^perp.
Since pi_V(int K)=int B, the condition F intersect int K empty is
equivalent to c outside int B. The density assertion and (4) prove
(2), with the exact rank r, not the ambient dimension D.

## 4. Sharpness

For (1), take K=T_r times L in V+V^perp, where T_r is an r-simplex
with centroid zero and L is any (D-r)-dimensional convex body (a
singleton if D=r). The r+1 canonical centroid vertex caps of T_r,
extended cylindrically, cover R^D, have normal rank r, and each has
fraction gamma_r of K. The homothety ratio of each simplex cap is
r/(r+1).

For (2) with r>=2, in R^r use

    E={(t,x):1<=t<=2, x in t T_(r-1)}.

Its exterior-contact caps through zero have fraction gamma_(r-1)
and initially rank r-1. To obtain rank exactly r and a unique
projected common contact, split one normal (0,beta_0) into
(epsilon,beta_0) and (-epsilon,beta_0), leaving all the other simplex
normals unchanged. Positive weights 1,1,2,...,2 balance them and
their span is R^r. Their largest cap fraction is exactly

    ((r-1)/r+epsilon)^(r-1),

which decreases to gamma_(r-1). Take the product with L. The common
flat {0} times R^(D-r) misses K, and this proves sharpness as an
infimum in the rank-r subclass. Replacing [1,2] by [0,1] gives the
boundary-contact version. For r=1, an interval times L with the two
endpoint-based opposite caps gives equality 1 exactly.

## 5. Consequences for an individual circuit

Fix one actual positive-volume mixed fiber K_z of volume w_z. If a
collection of ambient caps restricts to a whole-space cover on this
fiber and its continuous normals have rank r, one cap has TOTAL
mixed mass at least gamma_r w_z. Consequently a common total cap
bound <T implies

    w_z < T/gamma_r.                                     (7)

If those restricted caps have a common codimension-r boundary flat
missing int K_z, replace gamma_r in (7) by gamma_(r-1).
These are fiberwise incidence restrictions. They do not assert that
a heavy fiber exists, that different circuit contacts coincide, or
that a sum of fiberwise maxima is the maximum total mass of one cap.
